title: NGC 5291
caption: The collision-ringed galaxy NGC 5291 and the Seashell, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo
celestial: NGC 5291 · constellation Centaurus · about 200 million light-yearsz=0.014 (redshift) away (source figure)
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Acknowledgments: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Mahdi Zamani & Davide de Martin

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The hazy, golden oval at the center of this image is the elliptical galaxy NGC 5291. Faint, glowing clouds spread out to its left and right, forming a ring of debris left behind by a violent galactic collision.

More than 300 million years ago, NGC 5291 was struck by a rogue galaxy hurtling through space. The debris ring is the aftermath of that impact. NGC 5291 lies about 200 million light-years away, in the constellation Centaurus.

NGC 5291 is also part of a much gentler encounter. Just to the right of NGC 5291 is an unusually curved galaxy known as the Seashell, and the two are interacting calmly with each other. An elliptical galaxy is a smooth, rounded collection of stars without spiral arms, and collisions like this one show how violently such galaxies can be disturbed.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (13.16 x 10.63 arcminutes) and distance (200 million light yearsz=0.014 (redshift)), the frame spans roughly 766,000 × 618,000 light-years. Its light set out about 200 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo observed NGC 5291 through u, g, r and i filters, from near-ultraviolet through visible light to the edge of near-infrared. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The faint debris clouds are far too dim for the eye. The camera's exposures gather enough light to reveal them.
